chapters.title: Chapter 4: Country Risk and Your Portfolio

lessons.title: Diversifying Across Country Risk: What Indian Investors Get Wrong

children.text: Most of this course has looked at country risk through the eyes of foreign money deciding whether to invest in India. This lesson flips the camera around. If you are an Indian investor thinking about putting some money outside India, the same country risk framework applies to you directly, and a surprising number of otherwise sophisticated Indian investors get the basics wrong. Here are four specific mistakes worth avoiding.
Mistake One: Calling a US-Only Portfolio 'International Diversification'

The single most common pattern in Indian retail portfolios reaching for 'international exposure' is a Nasdaq 100 fund of funds or a US tech-heavy ETF, and nothing else. That is not wrong to own, but it is not diversification across country risk, it is swapping one single-country concentration (India) for another (the United States), often an even more concentrated one, given how heavily US index funds skew toward a handful of large technology companies. Genuine diversification across country risk means deliberately holding exposure across multiple, differently exposed economies, not just moving your single-country bet from one country to a different single country.
Mistake Two: Ignoring the Currency Bet Hiding Inside Every International Investment

Every time you move money abroad through the RBI's Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS), you are taking on the exact FX translation exposure from Chapter 3, just running in the opposite direction from a foreign investor buying Indian assets. The rupee has depreciated gradually against the dollar over most of the past few decades, which has historically added a modest tailwind to Indian investors' dollar-denominated holdings, on top of whatever the underlying US asset itself returned. It is a real mistake, however, to assume that trend continues automatically and indefinitely. A gradually depreciating currency is not a law of nature, it is itself a bet on continued relative macro performance, and India's own improving country risk story, covered across this entire course, is precisely the kind of development that could support a stronger rupee than history alone would suggest. Betting on rupee depreciation without realising you are making that bet is exactly the kind of unpriced currency risk this course has spent two chapters warning about, just facing the other direction.
Mistake Three: Treating 'Emerging Markets' as One Risk Bucket

A broad emerging markets equity or bond fund can quietly hold a mix of countries with wildly different risk profiles side by side: a BBB-rated, improving credit like India next to a frontier market still sitting deep in speculative-grade territory, well below investment grade. Recall from Chapter 2 exactly how much difference sits between the top and bottom of that spectrum, and from Chapter 3 what can happen at the bottom end of it. An investor who buys 'EM exposure' assuming it behaves as one homogenous risk bucket has skipped the entire three-pillar framework this course opened with. Look inside the fund's actual country weights before assuming you know what risk you are holding.
Mistake Four: Forgetting That India's Own Rules Are a Country Risk Factor Too

markDefs.definition: The RBI framework allowing resident Indian individuals to remit up to a specified amount abroad each financial year for permitted purposes, including investments in foreign securities.

children.text: This is the mistake most specific to Indian investors, and easiest to overlook. Your own ability to diversify abroad is itself shaped by India's capital account policy, which this course covered in Chapter 4's earlier lesson as a lever FIIs watch closely from the other direction. The

currently caps outward remittances at USD 250,000 per resident individual per financial year, and the tax treatment of these remittances has itself changed materially in recent years, including a 20% tax collected at source (TCS) on most LRS remittances for investment purposes above a specified annual threshold, effective from October 2023. Neither the limit nor the tax rate is fixed forever. Both are policy choices that can, and have, changed, which makes India's own regulatory stance a genuine country risk factor in your own diversification plan, not a fixed backdrop you can take for granted.

body.title: Spot the Flawed 'International' Portfolio
body.scenario: An investor tells you: 'I've diversified internationally. I put 15% of my portfolio into a US Nasdaq 100 fund of funds through the LRS route, on top of my existing India-heavy equity and mutual fund holdings. I plan to keep adding to it every year since the rupee always weakens against the dollar anyway.'
body.prompt: Using the four mistakes from this lesson, identify at least two flaws in this investor's reasoning.
body.modelAnswer: At least two mistakes are visible. First, Mistake One: this is not diversification across country risk, it is swapping India-concentration for US-concentration, and a Nasdaq 100 fund is itself heavily concentrated in a handful of large technology companies, arguably even less diversified than a broad India allocation. Second, Mistake Two: the investor is treating rupee depreciation as a guaranteed, permanent tailwind rather than a real, unhedged currency bet, exactly the trap this lesson warns against, especially given India's improving country risk profile covered throughout this course could support a stronger rupee than the investor is assuming. A genuinely diversified plan would spread exposure across multiple countries with different risk profiles and treat the currency exposure as a deliberate, sized decision rather than an assumed free tailwind.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: Why is buying a broad 'emerging markets' fund without checking its underlying country weights a potential mistake, based on this course?
options: Emerging market funds are not allowed to hold more than one country
All emerging markets carry identical country risk, so checking weights provides no useful information

Emerging markets span a wide range of credit ratings and risk profiles, from countries like India with an improving investment-grade story to others still deep in speculative-grade territory, so the fund's actual mix determines the real risk being taken
Emerging market funds always disclose their exact risk level in the fund's name
body.explanation: 'Emerging market' is a broad label covering countries with very different economic, political, and currency risk profiles, as this entire course has shown through the contrast between India's improving BBB-range credit story and Sri Lanka's 2022 default. An investor who assumes a labelled EM fund carries some single, uniform level of risk has skipped the actual analysis; the fund's specific country weights determine what risk is really being taken.

body.text: Diversifying across country risk means deliberately holding exposure to countries whose economic, political, and currency risks do not all move together, and consciously pricing every currency and policy assumption baked into that decision. Swapping one concentrated bet for another, or riding an assumed tailwind you never actually examined, is not diversification. It just feels like it.

children.text: The final lesson of this course pulls every idea covered so far, from the three-pillar framework to ratings, spreads, crisis anatomy, and now your own diversification decisions, into a single practical checklist you can run through before allocating money to any market outside your own.

points: A US-only 'international' allocation is not diversification across country risk, it is trading one single-country concentration for another, often a more concentrated one.

Every rupee moved abroad through the LRS carries a real, unhedged currency bet. Historical rupee depreciation is not a guaranteed future tailwind, especially given India's own improving country risk story.

'Emerging markets' is not a single risk bucket. Broad EM funds can span the full range from improving investment-grade credits to deep speculative-grade ones, and only checking the fund's actual country weights reveals the real risk.

India's own capital account rules, including the LRS limit and the tax treatment of outward remittances, are themselves a form of policy risk that shapes an Indian investor's ability to diversify, and can change.

Genuine diversification requires deliberately choosing exposures with different risk drivers and consciously pricing every currency and policy assumption, not assuming any of it is fixed or automatic.

body.text: The LRS limit and TCS rate cited in this lesson reflect rules as understood at the time of writing and are subject to change by the RBI and the government. Verify the current LRS limit, TCS thresholds and rates, and any other applicable regulations directly with the RBI, your bank's authorised dealer, or a tax professional before remitting funds abroad.
